title: USMCA not renewed: North America's trade pact moves to yearly reviews
deck: The United States declined to extend the continental trade deal for 16 years, so it now runs on a yearly review clock, and Washington is using that uncertainty to press Mexico and Canada on cars, China, steel and dairy.

card.headline: The USMCA still works, but it is now on a short leash with annual reviews until 2036

keyNumber.label: Mexico's trade surplus with the US in the year to August, up 51% (figure from the event summary)

forYou.line: The pact is in force, but car rules of origin and Chinese-content tests may tighten. Map which parts cross the border and where they originate.
Annual reviews turn every cycle into a headline risk for the peso, Canadian dollar and cross-border manufacturers.
Section 338 and Section 232 tariffs apply whatever the USMCA says, so origin status alone no longer protects you.
Cars, dairy and groceries are the most exposed goods. Price effects, if any, would build slowly.

effects.text: The US declined to confirm a 16-year extension at the 1 July 2026 joint review; the pact now expires on 1 July 2036 unless extended, with annual reviews until then
USTR opened the 2027 review on 2 October; written comments and hearing requests are due 12 January 2027
Mexico pledged on 13 October to buy more American goods to seek a bilateral deal
US demands focus on auto rules of origin, Chinese content, steel, dairy and trade deficits
Firms delay long-lived plant investment in Mexico and Canada until the rules are clearer
Mexico and Canada may split, with Mexico pursuing a bilateral track and Canada locked in a tariff fight
Suppliers redesign bills of materials to cut Chinese content and prove North American origin
Currency and equity markets react to each review headline
China tries to reach the US through other routes, and transshipment crackdowns raise costs for third countries
A Democratic House after the 3 November midterms could scrutinise any renegotiated text, slowing or reshaping a deal
North America's weaker trade certainty pushes some investment toward Asia and Europe, which face their own 2027 rules

whatHappened: At the first USMCA joint review on 1 July 2026, the United States declined to confirm a 16-year extension. Under Article 34.7, the pact therefore stays in force only to 1 July 2036 and must be reviewed every year.
USTR opened the 2027 review on 2 October. Written comments and hearing requests are due 12 January 2027. US demands centre on auto rules of origin, Chinese content, steel, dairy and trade deficits.
Mexico's trade surplus with the US rose 51% to over $280 billion in the year to August. On 13 October Mexico pledged to buy more American goods to secure a bilateral deal.
whyItMatters: The USMCA covers the most integrated supply chains in the world, especially cars. The pact is still in force, so nothing changes overnight. What changes is certainty: each year becomes a bargaining round.

Washington is using non-renewal alongside Section 338 tariffs as twin levers. Talks with Canada collapsed on 22 August after 50% Section 338 tariffs hit about $20 billion of Canadian goods. Alcohol and dairy imports from Canada were then banned from 29 September. Section 338 duties apply regardless of USMCA origin and stack on Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminium, autos and lumber.
Mexico is the most exposed. Its large surplus makes it the obvious target. It also has the most to lose if it fails to reach a deal.

winners.why: Annual reviews keep leverage permanently in play, and each cycle can win new concessions.

winners.who: US dairy, grain and other farm exporters
winners.why: Mexico's pledge to buy more American goods and US dairy demands point to wider market access.

winners.who: Producers with verifiably North American supply chains
winners.why: Tighter origin and anti-China rules favour firms that can document regional content.

losers.why: They face the largest US scrutiny, since the surplus is the political target, and a long period of investment uncertainty.

losers.who: Canadian dairy, alcohol and wine producers
losers.why: The US has banned or put 50% tariffs on these goods, and Canada has retaliated.
They face stricter rules of origin and Chinese-content tests while also paying steel and aluminium tariffs.

losers.who: Chinese exporters using Mexico as a route to the US
losers.why: US demands on Chinese content and transshipment target this channel.

whatsNext: 3 November 2026: US midterm elections. A Democratic House would change how Congress treats any renegotiated text.
12 January 2027: deadline for written comments and hearing requests in the USTR review.
Early 2027: hearings and USTR's assessment, then bilateral bargaining. Exact dates are not confirmed in our sources.
Annual reviews follow until 2036 unless all three countries confirm an extension.

predict.question: Before you read the scenarios: what is the most likely state of the USMCA a year from now?
options: All three countries agree to extend the pact to 2042
Still in force with annual reviews and a partial US-Mexico deal
The US gives notice to withdraw
The pact is replaced by two bilateral deals
predict.explanation: Our base case, at about 45%, is that the pact stays in force under annual review while Mexico trades concessions for relief. A clean extension is the least likely path, at about 10%, because US demands are broad and the Canada dispute is unresolved.

timeline.title: Iran war begins
timeline.detail: The fuel and grocery price rises that followed now dominate US politics and sharpen trade-deficit rhetoric.

timeline.title: First USMCA joint review
timeline.detail: The US declines to confirm a 16-year extension. Under Article 34.7 the pact now runs only to 1 July 2036, with annual reviews.

timeline.title: US-Canada talks collapse
timeline.detail: Washington imposes 50% Section 338 tariffs on about $20bn of Canadian goods: wine, furniture, dairy, cement, clothing.

timeline.title: Canadian alcohol and dairy duties become bans
timeline.detail: Trump signs five proclamations. Canada's Carney answers with dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs on US steel, dairy, appliances and farm equipment.

timeline.title: Canadian alcohol and dairy bans take effect
timeline.detail: Canadian products are also ordered off GSA procurement schedules.

timeline.title: USTR opens the 2027 review
timeline.detail: Written comments and hearing requests are due 12 January 2027.

timeline.title: Law-firm analysis: not renewed, still in force
timeline.detail: Mayo Law sets out what annual reviews mean in practice.

timeline.title: Mexico pledges to buy more American goods
timeline.detail: The aim is a bilateral deal. Mexico's surplus with the US rose 51% to over $280bn in the year to August.

timeline.title: US midterm elections
timeline.detail: All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are up. Democrats are favoured to take the House.

timeline.title: Comment and hearing-request deadline
timeline.detail: The formal record of the 2027 review closes, days after a new Congress convenes.

causes.name: Persistent US deficit with Mexico
causes.detail: A surplus above $280bn gives Washington a simple political target.

causes.name: China's presence in North American supply chains
causes.detail: The US wants to stop Chinese inputs and goods entering via Mexico or Canada.

causes.name: Built-in review clause
causes.detail: Article 34.7 turns non-confirmation into a lever without withdrawing from the pact.

causes.name: US declines to confirm extension
causes.detail: This switches the pact from a 16-year term to annual reviews ending in 2036.

causes.name: US-Canada tariff war
causes.detail: Section 338 tariffs, counter-tariffs and import bans show Washington will use tariffs outside the USMCA's rules.

causes.name: Rising Mexican surplus
causes.detail: A 51% rise in a year raised pressure on Mexico.

causes.name: US midterm politics
causes.detail: Gasoline and grocery prices push trade toughness and deficit messaging before 3 November.

stakeholders.name: Trump administration and USTR
stakeholders.wants: Lower deficits, tighter origin rules, less Chinese content, steel and dairy access
stakeholders.leverage: Annual non-renewal, Section 338 and Section 232 tariffs
stakeholders.likelyMove: Keep both countries under pressure; trade relief for concessions, mostly bilaterally

stakeholders.name: Mexican government (President Sheinbaum)
stakeholders.wants: Stable access to the US market and a bilateral deal
stakeholders.leverage: Purchases of American goods, control over Chinese investment and imports
stakeholders.likelyMove: Offer purchases and anti-China measures, avoid retaliation

stakeholders.name: Canadian government (Prime Minister Carney)
stakeholders.wants: An end to Section 338 tariffs and bans, and continued USMCA access
stakeholders.leverage: Counter-tariffs on US steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment
stakeholders.likelyMove: Hold the counter-tariffs while keeping the USMCA track open

stakeholders.name: US Congress
stakeholders.wants: Varies; Democrats favoured to win the House want scrutiny of any deal
stakeholders.leverage: Hearings and legislative review of changes
stakeholders.likelyMove: More hearings from January if the House changes hands

stakeholders.name: Automakers and parts suppliers
stakeholders.wants: Predictable origin rules and relief from stacked metal tariffs
stakeholders.likelyMove: File comments by 12 January, delay long-lived investment, redesign supply chains

stakeholders.name: China
stakeholders.wants: Keep export access via third countries
stakeholders.likelyMove: Shift routing and sourcing; avoid open confrontation

sectors.why: Rules of origin, Chinese content and steel and aluminium tariffs all hit the most integrated cross-border industry.
US demands on steel could lift some US producers, but tariffs raise costs for users.
US producers may gain access, while Canadian producers face a US import ban.

sectors.sector: Mexican industrial real estate and nearshoring
sectors.why: Uncertainty can delay new investment, though the pact remains in force.
Mexico's purchase pledge points to larger sales.
Annual reviews and origin audits raise demand for advisers.
Content and transshipment rules narrow indirect access to the US.

dailyLife.effect: Stacked tariffs and origin changes could raise costs for North American-built vehicles. The effect would build gradually.
Canadian alcohol and dairy imports to the US are banned from 29 September, so Canadian products disappear from US shelves. Canada's counter-tariffs raise prices on US dairy and goods there.
Prices are already high after the Iran war began on 28 February. Further tariffs or Mexican purchase deals may shift food costs, though the direction is uncertain.
Delayed investment and shifting origin rules weigh on hiring in Mexico and in US plants dependent on Mexican parts.
The peso and Canadian dollar may swing on review headlines, affecting travel and remittance costs.

scenarios.name: Annual-review limbo
scenarios.looksLike: The pact stays in force. USTR holds hearings, issues demands, and Mexico makes purchase and anti-China concessions in stages. Canada remains in dispute.
signposts: No extension announced after the January comments
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Steady uncertainty premium on North American investment; supply chains slowly re-document origin.

scenarios.name: US-Mexico bilateral deal
scenarios.looksLike: Mexico agrees purchases, tighter Chinese-content rules and steel measures in exchange for tariff relief and signals of a bilateral track.
signposts: Tariff relief on Mexican autos or steel
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Mexico stabilises, Canada isolated; the pact becomes less trilateral in practice.

scenarios.name: Escalation toward withdrawal
scenarios.looksLike: Talks fail, new tariffs hit Mexico, and Washington threatens notice of withdrawal.
signposts: Section 338 or similar tariffs on Mexican goods
Withdrawal rhetoric from the White House
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Severe disruption to the auto supply chain; recession risk across the three economies.

scenarios.name: Clean extension
scenarios.looksLike: A package resolves US demands and all three countries confirm a new 16-year term.
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Investment certainty returns; unlikely given the breadth of demands.

predictions.text: The USMCA will still be in force, with no withdrawal notice from any party (probability 0.9).
No three-country extension of the pact beyond 2036 will be confirmed (probability 0.9).
The US and Mexico will announce at least a partial bilateral trade arrangement tied to purchases or Chinese-content rules (probability 0.4).
US Section 338 tariffs on Canadian goods will remain in place on 12 January 2027 (probability 0.7).
Democrats will win control of the House in the 3 November midterms (probability 0.75, based on polling cited in the connected midterms dossier).

actions: File comments before 12 January if your supply chain crosses the border.
Map every part by country of origin and Chinese content share.
Model costs under tighter origin rules and stacked steel and aluminium tariffs.
Check contracts for tariff-pass-through and force-majeure terms.
Avoid sole reliance on one border crossing or Mexican plant for critical parts.
Treat the USMCA as a recurring annual risk event rather than a settled framework.
Watch peso and Canadian dollar reactions to review milestones and tariff announcements.
Check autos, parts and cross-border logistics holdings for dependence on Mexico and Chinese content.
Expect gradual price pressure on cars and some groceries, not a sudden shock.
If you plan a large vehicle purchase, compare North American-built and imported options.
Cross-border workers and remitters should watch exchange-rate swings.
Separate USMCA review issues from unrelated tariff measures to keep the pact predictable.
Coordinate Mexico-Canada positions where interests overlap, particularly on China.
Give firms early notice of origin-rule changes and transition periods.

analogues.whatFollowed: The US used tariff threats on steel and autos to win changes; the new pact was signed in 2018 and entered into force on 1 July 2020.

analogues.event: US tariff threat against Mexico over migration
analogues.whatFollowed: A threatened tariff was suspended after a June deal, showing how trade leverage can be used on unrelated goals.

analogues.event: Section 232 steel and aluminium tariffs on Canada and Mexico
analogues.whatFollowed: The tariffs were lifted in May 2019 as ratification of the new pact moved ahead, showing that relief is tradeable.

watch.title: US midterm elections
watch.why: A Democratic House would scrutinise any renegotiated text; the result sets the political backdrop for the review.

watch.title: Comments and hearing requests due
watch.why: The record of industry demands and objections closes; watch which sectors file and what they ask for.

watch.title: Section 338 tariffs on Canada
watch.why: Any extension of these tariffs to Mexico would signal escalation.

watch.title: Mexican purchase announcements
watch.why: Concrete purchase deals show whether the 13 October pledge is turning into a bilateral arrangement.

watch.title: EU CBAM and EUDR start dates
watch.why: Compliance resets in 2027 overlap with North American origin rules and may pull supply chains in different directions.
